**Patient Vignette: Mrs. A.**

Mrs. A. is a 42-year-old woman who presents for therapy at the urging of her primary care provider. She sits at the edge of the chair, her hands folded tightly in her lap, her gaze fixed on a spot on the floor. She speaks in a low, careful voice, as if afraid of being overheard.

The story begins five years ago, in her home country of Eritrea. Mrs. A. was a quiet woman, a mother of two, working as a seamstress. She had no interest in politics. But her younger brother had been part of a student group, and when the authorities came looking for him, they found her instead. She was taken to a detention center, a concrete room with no windows. For three weeks, she was held there. The men who questioned her wanted information she did not have. They used electricity, wires attached to her fingers and toes. They beat the soles of her feet with a rubber hose until she could no longer stand. They forced her to watch as they did the same to another woman, a stranger, who screamed until she went silent. Mrs. A. was released without explanation, her body a map of scars, her mind a shattered mirror.

She fled with her children, leaving her husband behind. He did not come with them; he said she was bringing shame on the family by leaving. They made their way to a refugee camp in Sudan, then to the United States three years ago. Now, she lives in a small apartment with her two children, works the night shift at a poultry processing plant, and tries to be invisible.

The factory is a nightmare she repeats every shift. The air is cold and damp, thick with the smell of bleach and blood. The machines hum and clatter, a constant, unpredictable noise. When a conveyor belt jams, a loud metallic bang echoes through the room. Mrs. A. flinches every time. Her heart races, her palms sweat, and she feels a cold dread slide down her spine. She has to press her hand against the wall to steady herself. Her supervisor, a well-meaning man, once touched her shoulder to get her attention. She spun around, her arm raised to strike, before she even knew what she was doing. She spent the rest of that shift in the bathroom, shaking, her breath coming in short, ragged gasps. She now makes sure she is never near him.

At home, she cannot sleep. She lies in bed, listening. A siren outside sends her crawling to the floor, her body pressed against the carpet, her mind back in that concrete room. She checks the locks on the door three times, then four, then a fifth. She has not had a full night’s sleep in four years. She avoids the news, avoids crowds, avoids the Eritrean community center because someone there might know her brother’s name. She has stopped calling her mother, who still lives in the old country. The guilt is a physical weight in her chest—guilt for leaving, guilt for surviving, guilt for the shame she brought on her family.

Her children are teenagers now. They speak English with a flat American accent. They do not know the details of what happened to her. She tells them only that she had a “hard time.” When her daughter asks about her father, Mrs. A. says nothing. She feels a vast, empty distance between herself and everyone she loves. She cannot feel joy. She cannot feel anger. Mostly, she feels nothing but a gray, buzzing numbness, punctuated by moments of sheer, animal terror.

She came to therapy because she had a panic attack in the grocery store last week. A man in a blue uniform—a security guard—was standing near the produce aisle. The color of his shirt, the way he stood with his legs apart, the way he looked at her—it was the same. She dropped her basket and ran. She ran all the way home, her children’s faces a blur in her mind. She knows she cannot keep running. But she does not know how to stop.
